newsitem.title: UK: Full text of September 23 UK monetary minutes.
newsitem.headline: Full text of September 23 UK monetary minutes.

text.p: The following is the complete text of the minutes of the September 23 monthly monetary policy meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England governor Eddie George.
The Chancellor of the Exchequer and the Governor of the Bank of England met, together with officials, on 23 September, to review monetary developments.
Monetary and Economic Developments

2. Latest monetary and economic data (reviewed by officials before the meeting) provided further evidence that cost and price pressures remained moderate. However, there were signs that output growth had started to pick up, and recent indicators of business confidence and consumer demand were more buoyant.
Inflation Indicators

3. Underlying inflation (RPI excluding mortgage interest payments - RPIX) was unchanged in August, at 2.8 per cent, for the fourth successive month. All-items RPI inflation fell by 0.1 percentage point, to 2.1 per cent.
4. Most other price and cost indicators confirmed that inflationary pressures remained moderate:
- sterling's effective exchange rate index rose by 0.3 in the period since the last meeting, to stand at 86.1;
- producer input prices for manufacturing (excluding food, beverage, tobacco and petroleum industries) rose in August by 0.1 per cent; but compared to a year ago they were 6.6 per cent lower;
- however, the oil price had risen again slightly to $22.2 per barrel, reflecting continued tensions in the Middle East;

- producer output prices (excluding FBTP) were unchanged in August; but the annual inflation rate fell to 1.2 per cent, from 1.4 per cent in July. The CBI survey output price expectations balance increased slightly in September, but remained at a low level;
- the annual growth rate of underlying average earnings was unchanged in July, at 3 per cent.
Monetary and Financial Indicators

5. No new M0 data had been published since the last meeting, although provisional and partial information suggested that growth had fallen back again following the sharp rise in August. M4 grew by 0.9 per cent in August, up from 0.5 per cent in July; and the annual growth rate rose to 9.4 per cent, from 9.0 per cent in July. Growth in M4 lending was 0.6 per cent in August, down from 0.7 per cent in July.

6. No new data on house prices were available since the last meeting. Housing market transactions continued to recover; particulars delivered (which lag actual transactions) in the three months to August were 6.4 per cent up on the previous three months, and 9.1 per cent up on a year earlier.

7. Short-term interest rates were little changed in the US and Japan since the last meeting, but had fallen slightly in Germany. UK short-term interest rates were little changed. Forward interest rates implicit in short-sterling futures contracts increased by around 20 basis points for December 1996, but had fallen by around 10 basis points at the long end.

8. 10-year bond yields had fallen by around 15 basis points in the US and Japan, and by around 25 basis points in Germany. In the UK, yields on conventional gilts had also fallen at all maturities (by up to 15 basis points). Since the last meeting inflation expectations implied by the gilt yield curve (calculated by the Bank from the difference between the yields on conventional and index-linked bonds) had fallen by nearly 20 basis points for both 5 and 10 years ahead.
Activity Indicators

9. In the US recent data indicated that activity remained buoyant. The August employment numbers were again strong, and unemployment fell to 5.1 per cent - the lowest level since March 1989. Industrial production rose by 0.5 per cent in August, following a rise of 0.1 per cent in July. The latest estimate of US GDP growth in Q2 was 1.2 per cent, leaving it 2.7 per cent up on a year earlier. In Japan GDP was estimated to have fallen in Q2 by 0.7 per cent, although this was largely a response to the very strong rise in Q1.

10. Indicators in Europe were mixed. In Germany GDP was provisionally estimated to have grown in Q2 by 1.5 per cent, leaving it 1.1 per cent up on a year earlier. However, in France GDP was estimated to have fallen by 0.4 per cent in Q2, following a rise of 1.2 per cent in Q1.

11. No new UK GDP data had been published since the last meeting. Other activity data were consistent with a pick-up in demand, and more forward-looking indicators of business confidence and consumer demand remained strong:

- manufacturing output rose by 0.5 per cent in July. However, in the three months to July it was down 0.1 per cent on a year earlier. Total industrial output rose by 0.5 per cent in July, and in the latest three months was up 1.0 per cent on a year earlier;
- retail sales rose by 1.0 per cent in August, following a fall of 0.6 per cent in July. In the three months to August sales were 3.5 per cent higher than in the same period a year earlier;

- survey indicators in the retail sector remained strong: consumer confidence rose slightly, and in the August CBI Distributive Trades Survey the balance of retailers expecting higher sales rose further, and remained at a high level by historical standards;
- claimant unemployment fell by 15,600 in August, to its lowest level since March 1991, and unfilled vacancies at Jobcentres increased by 6,400.
Summary of Discussion

12. The Governor said that it was less than 3 weeks since the last meeting. There had nevertheless been significant new data which provided fairly solid further evidence of the gathering economic momentum that the Bank had been projecting for some time.

13. Short-term cost and producer price developments remained favourable overall in August. Producer input prices (s.a) in fact picked up by 0.3 per cent on the month (after rising by 0.2 per cent in July), mainly due to higher oil prices - but they remained 2.1 per cent below their level of a year ago. The relative strength of the exchange rate - if it persisted - would help to contain any immediate pick-up. And producer output prices were for the time being effectively flat - with the year-on-year rate of growth still falling (+2 per cent in August). Pay settlements appeared still to be running at around 3-1/2 per cent; and underlying earnings growth remained at 3-3/4 per cent in the year to July - unchanged since February - with the rate of growth in manufacturing (+4 per cent) and in services (+3-3/4 per cent) apparently converging.

14. Retail price inflation, measured by RPIX, remained stubbornly at 2.8 per cent year on year - for the fifth month in a row (after correcting for the ONS error). It was not clear exactly why this had happened, but the Bank was now less confident that underlying inflation would in fact fall to within the target over the next few months.

15. Turning to demand and output, the Governor noted that revised GDP estimates had just been received which included significant upward revisions to Q1 and Q2 GDP growth (+0.6 per cent and +0.5 per cent respectively, compared with the earlier estimates of +0.4 per cent in each quarter). The revisions also suggested that net trade had been stronger in H1, which together with an improving outlook on the continent, especially in Germany, pointed to less of a drag on output than earlier seemed possible. The downward adjustment of stocks in relation to output in Q2 was now seen to be somewhat larger than on initial estimates; and there had been upward revisions to investment and personal consumption offset by downward revisions to public consumption, which now put final domestic demand growth annualised since Q4 at 4 per cent.

16. Retail sales volumes had risen very strongly in August (by 1 per cent on the month, to a level 4.4 per cent higher than a year earlier); and there had been upward revisions for earlier months, giving a three-month increase of 1.6 per cent - the strongest since August 1988. Surveys and anecdotal evidence confirmed the picture of buoyant consumption growth, with the August CBI Distributive Trades Survey reporting retailers' sales expectations at their highest level since end-1988, and an increasing proportion of retailers expecting to increase orders to suppliers. House prices had continued to increase in August (with both Halifax and Nationwide reporting annual house price inflation above 5 per cent), particulars delivered rose (by 3 per cent) in August, and mortgage lending increased.

17. Industrial production (+0.5 per cent) and manufacturing output (also +0.5 per cent) both recovered in July, having fallen in June (by 0.8 per cent and 0.1 per cent respectively); and the increases in output expectations in the July and August CBI surveys had been sustained in September. New car registrations had been below trade expectations in August, although the CBI Distributive Trades Survey reported that motor traders' sales remained high.

18. The Governor said that narrow money growth had picked up over the June-August period. The average monthly growth rate of notes and coin was 0.7 per cent over that period, compared with 0.6 per cent a month during the first five months of the year. The pick-up in notes and coin growth was consistent with other data suggesting a strengthening of high street spending over the summer.

19. Broad money had grown by 0.9 per cent in August (compared with 0.5 per cent in July), for a year-on-year change of 9.4 per cent (against 9 per cent in July). M4 lending growth, on the other hand, was modestly slower: monthly growth was 0.6 per cent compared with 0.7 per cent in July, but year-on-year growth rose to 9.1 per cent, from 8.9 per cent in July.

20. The Governor concluded that the data since the 4 September meeting had strengthened the case for raising rates to 6 per cent, and that was the Bank's advice. It was of course possible that the latest data were erratically strong. While demand was rather clearly on an upward trend, output may still be held back for a time by further downward stock adjustment, though the Q2 data made that seem less likely. A case could always be made for delay. But if the buoyancy of the last month's data was to be confirmed over the five weeks to the next meeting, it might become necessary to tighten policy more sharply.

21. The Chancellor said there had been some new information since the last meeting which had made the economic picture clearer. The most significant new information had been the revisions to GDP growth in the first and second quarters of 1996. GDP growth was now recorded as 0.6 per cent in 1996 Q1 and 0.5 per cent in 1996 Q2. These revised figures accorded more closely with how he had viewed activity at the time, whereas the first published figures had shown 0.4 per cent growth in each quarter. This was further evidence that there was a reasonable recovery underway. Any downside risk of a long period of below trend growth had significantly declined.

22. The Chancellor expected the recovery to continue through the year, and there were no signs of inflationary pressures re-emerging. In retrospect, the upward revisions to activity made it easier to understand why retail price inflation had not so far come down by as much as producer price inflation. He had been right to revise down the growth forecast for 1996 from 3 per cent at the time of the last Budget. But the summer economic forecast of 2-1/2 per cent growth for the year, which some commentators had thought too optimistic, was now looking 23. The upward revisions to GDP growth were in line with his expectations earlier in the year, and still showed the economy growing slightly below trend. The manufacturing data had been more encouraging: output was up 0.5 per cent in July, after falling slightly in June. It now seemed clear that the manufacturing sector had slowed in the first half of the year, but was now growing again. The service sector continued to perform well.

24. The Chancellor said that the housing market was becoming a little stronger. The increase in house prices was now more broadly based. He noted that particulars delivered had risen to over the 100,000 mark in August, but this was by no means remarkable by historical standards. Consumer activity also seemed to be rising as expected. Retail sales were becoming quite strong, up 1.6 per cent in the three months to August on the previous three months, although the increase on a year ago was a more modest 3.5 per cent.

25. The Chancellor said that the data on costs and prices remained good, although RPI inflation had not so far followed producer prices down as much as expected. Earnings growth and commodity price pressures remained moderate and underlying producer output price inflation was the lowest for 30 years. The exchange rate remained firm. Monetary growth had picked up a little. M0 growth had increased slightly in August. M4 growth had also risen, to 9.4 per cent, just outside its monitoring range.

26. The Chancellor said the overall picture was that demand had strengthened, led by the retail and consumer sectors. But in his view there had not been a fundamental change in the overall picture of activity since the last meeting.
27. In discussion the following points were made:

- domestic demand, in particular on the consumer side, had picked up sharply in recent months, consistent with strong growth of the money supply. This had only just started to be reflected in output growth, particularly in manufacturing; but the risks of growth continuing below trend had fallen in the light of the most recent data;

- retail inflation had not fallen back in recent months as would have been expected, given the good performance on producer prices and earnings growth. Retailers may be taking advantage of strong consumer demand to raise prices, although there were still strong pressures on firms to remain competitive;

- although the judgment on interest rates was finely balanced, there were advantages in acting preemptively (as had happened in 1994): raising rates early could mean that they had to rise by less; and it would send a clear message to price- and wage-setters that the Government was fully committed to meeting the inflation target. There were also benefits in moving rates in small steps. Futures prices were currently discounting a 1/4 percentage point rise in rates by December.
Conclusion

28. Summing up the Chancellor said that he felt that the case for a rise in interest rates was not yet proven. There were no signs of inflationary pressures re-emerging. Even after the GDP revisions, output growth was close to, but not above, trend. However, as he had made clear at previous meetings, if the picture changed to a point where the chances were that the inflation target would not be met, he would not hesitate to raise interest rates.

29. The Chancellor said that there would be considerably more data available at the next meeting in five weeks time, but in his view, the evidence since the last meeting was not enough to justify a move in interest rates. He decided to leave interest rates unchanged for the moment.
H M Treasury
